summary:
My son: Imagine we got to see all the cool stuff NASA left behind in space as if we were a astronaut.
Me: Imagine ??, we don't imagine , we build !!

I have built a VR enabled 3D first person experience of the solar system with all the abandoned tech NASA left behind (At their current position). Its like an open world game (Like Minecraft) where the user decides where he/she goes (yes it has sound effects too :) ).  No kid wants to hear a story , they want to live the story and thats exactly what this platform does. With high resolution 3D animations of planets the user can move anywhere by pointing towards the planet or the object and with a click they travel there. The platform flashes the user with a info card containing its real picture, name, location, current status, and why it matters with a fun fact about it all while you see a real time 3D animation of it. bored with this one ? , The View objects tab provides you a list of 22 abandoned objects enabling you to directly view it without looking at the map. The best part is you can connect this platform with your VR Headset and experience it to its fullest. 

This platform doesn't solve a problem , yes you heard that right, It provides you with an experience. An experience of being the cool uncle to your space enthusiast nephew 
(Not a Mark Rober reference)

Hon’ble Judge, if you are seeing this , I hope i can get a personal feedback about my project :) 
my mail : pranavkaushik213@gmail.com

Will make you proud one day !
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Ever wanted to be an astronaut without the 7 years of training? Yeah, me too. So I built it.

It’s a first-person, VR-ready flight through the Solar System, and the stars of the show are the 22 machines NASA abandoned out there (sitting at their real spots). You start near Earth and fly wherever you like. W, A, S, D and the mouse steer, and scrolling is your throttle. Every machine has a glowing beacon. Point at one, click, and a warp whooshes you straight to it.

You land next to a 3D model of the machine, and an info card pops up with its real NASA photo, its mission, its timeline, whether it’s still alive, and why it matters. Don’t know where to go? The View Objects button lists all 22, so you can teleport without hunting around. Oh, and it has music and sound effects, because silence in space is overrated. :)

What benefits does it have?

  • No textbook, no boring slides. You learn by flying there.
  • Runs in a browser. No downloads, and the headset is optional.
  • Every fact comes from NASA, and every card has a link to the source.
  • It gives lonely machines visitors. Spirit has been silent since 2010, and now someone drops by.

What is the intended impact?

I want a kid to go “WAIT, THERE’S A HELICOPTER ON MARS?!” and then lose an hour exploring for more. It doesn’t solve a problem (yes, again), it hands you a moment of wonder. If one kid walks away curious about space, mission accomplished. And if you’re the cool uncle, you now have a cheat code.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with a bit of Node.js for the asset downloader.
  • 3D and VR: three.js for the 3D world, and WebXR so it works with VR headsets.
  • Sound: the Web Audio API. The music and whoosh are generated in code, so there are no audio files.
  • Data: NASA’s NSSDCA catalog, NASA mission pages and the NASA Image Library, plus free planet textures from Solar System Scope.
  • Deploy and gear: GitHub, Vercel, and one MacBook Air held together by coffee.
  • AI sidekick: Claude helped me write and test the code. (Honesty is a feature too.)

How is it creative?

Most space education shows you a story. This one lets you live it. No timeline to read, no video to watch. You are the pilot, and the abandoned machines are the secrets you discover. I also flipped the usual angle: everyone celebrates the active missions, so I went for the forgotten ones. Instant emotional hook. Add the warp jump, the lit planets, and a soundtrack that reacts to your speed, and it stops feeling like a website and starts feeling like a game.

What factors did your team consider?

My team is just me, so basically everything. 😄

  • Accuracy: Real landing sites, NASA data and a source link on every card. I also checked each fact against NASA’s own pages.
  • Scale: A real-size Solar System would take forever to cross, so I squished the distances and made the machines bigger so you can actually spot them.
  • Audience: Short, friendly text for kids, and just WASD to learn.
  • Not hiding the good stuff: The “View Objects” button is right there, so nobody needs to guess a secret shortcut.
  • Speed: It runs in a browser, and photos load only when you need them.
  • Plan B: If a photo or texture doesn’t load, the site shows a backup instead of crashing.
